label: paragraph_title
text: HIVE CAREERS.

label: paragraph_title
text: LIFE TASK OF THIRTY-FIVE

label: text
text: Some time ago a famous German entomologist, Professor Karl von Frisch, constructed a beehive with glass windows and watched the bees "talking" to one another by means of special dances.

label: text
text: His pupil, Mr. G. A. Rosch, using the same technique has been able to observe, the entire career of several bees, from the moment they emerged from their pupae cells to the day of their death.

label: text
text: As soon as the young worker been appeared they were carefully removed from the hive, and marked by "spots of specially prepared paint. They were then put back, and each became as she set about her career, could be watched and tried among the hundreds of her sisters.

label: text
text: It is now established that the life of the average bee is a short and a hard one. She goes through a routine very similar to that of a human being, though it is compressing within a much shorter span. She seldom lives longer than 35 days, though veterans aged 55 days, have been recorded.

label: text
text: He's first task, after she has thoroughly washed and cleaned herself, is to prepare the cells for those who will follow after.

label: text
text: At the age of 3 to 10 days the young worker helps the regular nurses to feed the larvae. She fetches honey and pollen from the common store, and she also busies herself with the cleaning of the hive by carrying all foreign bodies outside it, and often helps the young to creep out of their cells by biting through their lids.

label: text
text: When she is about a fartnight old she takes over a post of great responsibility. She becomes a sentry. With a sagacity almost equal to that of a fully trained human soldier, she keeps her guard, watching over all bees coming in or going out, and if necessary doing battle with rash or straying marauders who endeavour to gain access to the treasure within.

label: text
text: As a rule, the bee becomes a honey gatherer round about the 20th day of her life; but the period may vary a little.

label: text
text: The observations of Mr. Rosch have definitely proven that the routine for all worker bees is the same, and that each one, if necessary, and according to her age, can take over any job in the communal life at short notice.

label: paragraph_title
text: YOUTH REPRIEVED.

label: text
text: When a "Sunday Chronicle" reporter visited the reprieved boy's home at Highbury he found the mother who had hoped and prayed that somehow at the last moment their son's life would be spared prostrate in bed overcome with joy.

label: text
text: Mrs. Kopsch received "notification of the Home Secretary's decision in dramatic fashion. About half past six on Friday evening, while awaiting Mr. Kopsch's return from work, she saw a clergyman come to the door. He was a stranger, and her thoughts turned instinctively to her son.

label: text
text: "I am from Pentonville," announced the stranger, who was, indeed, the prison chaplain, and the mother went cold with anxiety. "Is it about my son?" she hardly dared to ask.

label: paragraph_title
text: Overjoyed.

label: text
text:
by the hand and said comfortingly. "Now bear up. I come with good news. Your son is reprieved."
It was an overjoyed excited mother who greeted Mr. Kopsch when he arrived home. "Have you heard the news?" she asked, and scarcely waiting for a reply exclaimed, "Freddie's reprieved." The father stood silent for a few terrible moments wondering, doubting, whether the thing was true or some cruel hoax. Then when convinced that Freddie really had been spared his emotions got the better of him and with a muttered but grateful "Thank God," he burst into tears.

label: text
text: “Freddie's” chum, Maurice Williams, volunteered to go to Pentonville where he confirmed the reprieve decision and obtained a pass for Mr. Kopsch to see the boy.

label: text
text: Until a week before the mother received almost daily letters written by "Freddie" in jail, and it was significant that in mail week there had been no letters or message of any description.

label: text
text: Rut to a mother, who thought only of the boy whom she had brought into the world, the chaplain's mission of mercy was worth all the letters ever written.

label: text
text: Auntie had come to stay, and little Mary, with some pride, was showing a jumper she had knitted herself.

label: text
text: "And did my little niece make this all by herself?" asked auntie. "Nearly," was the reply. All but the hole you put your head through, and that was there before I started."

label: paragraph_title
text: SOUTH SEA LIFE

label: text
text: Over 1,300 rare species of insects, many of them undoubtedly now discoveries, have been brought to London by Mias L. E. Cheesman, curator of insects at the London 200.

label: text
text: INSECTS GREAT AND SMALL

label: text
text: She went to the South Seas with the expeditionary research ship "St. George," and after a year's voyaging among remote islands made a thorough exploration of the wild parts of Tahiti, Raia, and Bora Bora. "Hitherto insects had been collected only in the cultivated parts of Tahiti," she said.

label: text
text: "The astonishing thing we have to explain is how some of the species established themselves on these islands. Many are quite delicate creatures, and yet they contrived to cross thousands of miles of sea—in some cases, no doubt, in plants and so forth."

label: text
text: "Among them are the tiny Embids, which five in little silken tunnels in the bark of trees," and the brilliantly "coloured Plant Bugs, some only an eighth of an inch in size. Most of the species are small, and required a great deal of searching for." a hard morning's work would frequently produce only a dozen specimens.

label: text
text: Miss Cheesman found great danger from scorpions and centipedes. In places she encountered giant arum lilies with leaves as big as umbrellas and blossoms two feet in length.

label: text
text: In Trinidad, she said, she found a man who sold giant centipedes by the foot! Where they exceeded a foot in length, you paid for the extra inches in proportion.

label: paragraph_title
text: IS SCIENCE CRUEL?

label: paragraph_title
text: CIVILIZATION AND THE DEATH-RATE

label: text
text: POISON GAS v. SEWERS

label: text
text: It is really true that it is far more dangerous to life and limb to cross the Strand than the Channel, and a hundred times more perilous than a railway journey to Edinburgh, asserts a "Daily Mirror" writer.

label: text
text: The hall-mark of the highest civilisation, to motor-car, in its multifarious embodiments, has increased the death rate of road and street enormously.

label: text
text: The sense of disillusionment oppressing the world, proceeds the writer, arises mainly from a sense of profound disappointment with civilisation. It did not rise to the great occasion. Instead of science, for instance, mitigating the horrors of war, it appears to intensify them. So far from universal education having turned men into angles it seems to have had an effect the exact reverse. The civilised usages of warfare make the Romans, for instance, seem like philanthropists. Nevertheless, is there another side to the shield?

label: text
text: If civilisation kills, it also makes alike; if it is ruthless, it is also merciful. Even in the late war the proportion of those engaged who succumbed was smaller far than formerly, although the aggregate was so large. But had the microbe had its way, as in former wars, that terrible four years would have nearly depopulated the world of its men-folk.

label: text
text: Science may produce poison gas in time of war, but it is down on poison sewers, poison drains and poison food in time of peace.

label: paragraph_title

SEARCH IN HOUSE OF
COUNTESS.

label: text
text: Scotland Yard detectives investigated a reported robbery at 1, eamore-place, Park-lane, W., the residence of Almina Countess of arnarvon and her husband, t.-Col. Ian Dennistoun.

label: text
text: An alarm was given that intruders had been seen in the house. The police were called in and a room-to-room search was decided on. The house extends in the rear to Park-lane, and it is believed that the intruders entered by the back. Some articles, but no jewellery, were found to be missing in the early stage of the search.

label: text
text: Mud Marks/in the Hall.

label: text
text: The missing property consists of a quantity of valuable Georgian silver articles. In response to a telephone message from the house to Scotland Yard, detective visited the mansion to solve the mystery of what appeared to be a robbery carried out in a mysterious manner.

label: text
text: The detectives continued their investigations and the rear portion of the house was closely examined

label: text
text: for any traces of an entry having been forced by scaling cluster pipes and entering by a window.

label: text
text: The search was made in the hope of finding finger-prints.

label: text
text: Mud-marks found in the hall and on the stairs led to a theory that a man had in some way opened the front door and proceeded to the room where the silver was kept.

label: paragraph_title
text: LIFE OF PLANTS.

label: text
text: DRINKING WATER AND POISON

label: paragraph_title
text: THE TREE'S "HEART."

label: text
text: Three important discoveries which Sir J. D. Bose demonstrated in Calcutta are considered by scientists as of profound significance in developing our knowledge of the evolutionary process of life. Sir J. D. Fose, in the presence of the Earl of, Lytton and a distinguished gathering, explained his discovery of the muscular system in plants, and demonstrated the throbbing activity in the interior of trees.

label: text
text: Actual heart of the tree by means of an electric probe in conjunction with a sensitive galvanometer. As soon as the probe was put in contact with the heart, electric signals were automatically recorded by the galvanometer. The heart of plants is similar to the elongated heart of some of the lower animals, such as the earthworm. In an amazing demonstration, Sir J. D. Bose, by means of intricate instruments magnifying 5,000 times, showed the exhilarating effect of plants imbibing water containing small doses of ether as a stimulant, and finally he poisoned them with a fatal dose of potassium cyanide, the struggle ending in a rapid and spasmodic fall of the leaves indicating death throes. Sir J. D. Bose will proceed to London to prove his latest discoveries before the Royal Society, of which he is a member.

label: paragraph_title
text: JAUNTY MUSIC.

label: paragraph_title
text: MODES OF ELDERS:

label: paragraph_title
text: NOT TOO ELEGANTLY GAY!

label: text
text: Jauntiness seems to be the mode with the youngest of the young musical composers these days. It is a reaction against the modes of their elders—the finished elegance of Ravel and the direminess of Debussy. Ravel is an antique. Debusslam is a cons away, along with nineteenth-century "souffulness," writes Richard Capell, in the "Daily Mail." As a motorist might look on a Romain chariot, so do they consider Wagner and Beethoven.

label: text
text: They declare war on the Profound, the Nobles and the Pathetic. They want a gay music—but not too elegantly gay; rather, cheeky and "legpulling." When the mode was romantic, naturally cheerful young men felt bound to affect a broken heart and to look consumptive. But such a 1925 musician as M. Georges Auric is never to be found in the hour of twilight leaning pensively over the wall of a cemetery. No; he would rather go off boisterously to the circus, and if the cornet in the band persists in misreading the key-signature, it is an inspiration.

label: text
text: The new jainty music is a protest against sham sentiment and the obscurity which conceals hollowness. It may be raucous and crude, but it is frank and unpretentious. Quite often it is very clever, and at its best, as in some of Prokoviev's music, it is clearly spontaneous and exhilaratingly merry.

label: paragraph_title
text: WHISKY IN BIBLES.

label: paragraph_title
text: MILLIONAIRE DRUNK AS "BOILED OWL:"

label: text
text: LADY GOVERNOR TALKS.

label: text
text: A somewhat humorous situation has developed in the State of Texas, with Mrs. Miriam A. Ferguson, its governor, as the central figure.

label: text
text: Her enemies, whom she identifies with the Ku Klux Klan, threatened to violate the rules of political chivalry by impeaching her for undue sentimentality in pardoning more than 1,000 convicts. To this she has replied by issuing a proclamation offering $100 reward for the arrest and conviction of any rich citizen committing crimes for which poor people have been sent to jail.

label: text
text: In the proclamation and in interviews explaining its necessity, after dwelling on the case of a labourer of 18 who was sent to jail for sharing a "thin pint of corn whisky" with a friend behind a hedge, Mrs. Ferguson thus describes a big party given by a multimillionaire oil magnate.

label: text
text: "Why, he had his garage fitted up like a regular bar, with brass rallings and sawdust on the floor. He gave a dinner at which 600 pints of liquor were drunk and to his guests he presented as souvenirs 800 imitation Bibles and 300 canoes each containing a pint of whiskey."

label: text
text: The governor proceeded to state that the same millionaire appeared at a football match on Thanksgiving Day, "drunk as a bolled owl and waving his came, presumably filled with liquor."

label: text
text: Mrs. Ferguson also publicly accuses a district judge of drinking boot-leg whisky a few moments after sentencing to imprisonment a batch of boot-leggers.
